summary.text: A tundra is a biome where freezing temperatures and short growing seasons hold back the growth of trees.
Its permanently frozen ground stores large amounts of dead plant matter as methane and carbon dioxide, which makes tundra soil a carbon sink.
When warming thaws that ground, the stored gases escape into the air and feed further climate change in a loop.

facts.label: Yearly precipitation
facts.value: Only about 150–250 mm, like a polar desert

items.prompt: Arctic tundra gets about as little precipitation as a desert, yet in summer it is dotted with lakes and marshes. Why?

options.label: Heavy summer storms dump most of the year's rain at once
Frozen ground below stops the water from draining away
Melting glaciers nearby flood the low plains each summer
Sea water spills inland during the long summer days

items.explain: In summer only the top layer thaws; the permafrost underneath keeps water from sinking deeper, so it pools into lakes and marshes.

items.prompt: A forester plants young spruce on the Arctic tundra. What mainly stops them from growing into trees?

options.label: The soil holds too little nitrogen for roots
Reindeer herds graze every sapling flat
The ground is frozen a short way down
Summer days are too dark for leaves

items.explain: The soil is frozen from 25 to 90 cm down, which makes tree growth impossible; the soil itself is actually rich in nitrogen.

items.prompt: Warming thaws a stretch of tundra permafrost. What happens to the carbon that was locked in its soil?

options.label: It escapes as greenhouse gases that add to warming
It sinks deeper and is buried for good
It turns into nitrogen that feeds new plants
It stays put because thawing only affects water

items.explain: Thawing speeds up the permafrost carbon cycle and releases stored methane and carbon dioxide, which feeds back into climate change.

items.prompt: You might expect Russia's, Canada's and Alaska's record cold to have been set on the open Arctic tundra. Where was it actually recorded?

options.label: On the treeless tundra near the Arctic coast
On high alpine tundra above the mountains
Out on frozen sea ice beyond the shore
South of the tree line, in the taiga

items.explain: Tundra cold extremes generally don't reach as low as those in the taiga further south, where these countries' lowest temperatures were recorded.

items.prompt: An oil pipeline was built across tundra decades ago. What climate-change threat does it face from the ground itself?

options.label: Deeper snow each winter crushing the pipe
Frozen soil beneath it thawing and shifting
Rising groundwater rusting it from below
New forests pushing their roots under it

items.explain: Climate change thaws permafrost, and that thaw is a significant risk to roads and pipelines built on top of it.

items.prompt: Tundra has few kinds of land mammals. Which animals arrive there by the millions each year?

options.label: Frogs and lizards from the south
Brown bears from the forests
Sea turtles to lay their eggs
Migrating birds for the marshes

items.explain: Millions of birds migrate to the tundra each year for its marshes, while cold-blooded animals like frogs and lizards are largely absent.

paragraphs.heading: Land where trees give up
paragraphs.text: A tundra is a biome in which bitter cold and short growing seasons hold trees back. There are three kinds: Arctic, Alpine and Antarctic. The plant cover is made up of dwarf shrubs, sedges, grasses, mosses and lichens, though scattered trees grow in some tundra areas. The border zone where tundra meets forest is called the tree line or timberline.

paragraphs.heading: Frozen ground below
paragraphs.text: The word usually means land whose subsoil is permafrost, ground that stays frozen all the time. Arctic tundra is frozen for much of the year, and its soil is frozen from 25 to 90 cm down, which makes it impossible for trees to grow. In summer the top layer thaws and the ground turns soggy, dotted with marshes, lakes, bogs and streams. The frozen layer underneath stops the meltwater from sinking deeper, so it pools at the surface instead.

paragraphs.heading: Cold, windy and dry
paragraphs.text: Polar tundra has two main seasons, winter and summer. Winters are cold, dark and windy, averaging around −28 °C and sometimes reaching −50 °C. Summer days usually warm to about 12 °C but often fall to 3 °C or even below freezing. Winds often blow at 50–100 km/h. The tundra also counts as a polar desert, with only about 150–250 mm of precipitation a year, but little water evaporates either.

paragraphs.heading: Who lives there
paragraphs.text: Few kinds of living things manage here. There are about 1,700 species of vascular plants and only 48 land mammal species, plus a few fish, though millions of birds arrive each year for the marshes. Animals include reindeer, musk ox, Arctic hare, Arctic fox, snowy owl, lemmings and mosquitoes, with polar bears near the ocean, while animals like frogs and lizards are largely missing. People live here too, mostly nomadic reindeer herders such as the Nenets and Nganasan.

paragraphs.heading: A carbon store at risk
paragraphs.text: Tundra soil is rich in nitrogen and phosphorus, and its permafrost holds a great deal of dead plant matter stored as methane and carbon dioxide. That makes the soil a carbon sink, a store of carbon. As global warming thaws the ground, these greenhouse gases escape into the air, which adds to climate change in a feedback loop. Thawing also threatens roads and pipelines built on frozen ground, and it could change which species can survive there.

paragraphs.heading: Fire on the tundra
paragraphs.text: Fire is part of the picture too. Research in Alaska found that fires return about every 150 to 200 years, with drier lowlands burning more often than wetter highlands. Where dead plants and peat pile up, wildfire becomes a risk: in 2007, 1,039 km² of tundra burned on the north slope of Alaska's Brooks Range. Fires like this can both result from global warming and feed it.
